content: Organizations involved in specific areas of public health should clearly define their roles and responsibilities, ideally in collaboration with local authorities or international organizations such as the World Health Organization (WHO). This process should also address any discrepancies in standards of practice. Efforts must be coordinated with local authorities and healthcare providers to prevent foreign agencies from diverting critical resources away from essential services. Foreign aid workers should only be deployed if they possess the necessary skills to provide services that are not adequately available in the local setting. Deploying unqualified or unnecessary workers solely to fulfill personal or professional aspirations, often referred to as disaster tourism, is inappropriate. Prospective foreign aid workers must be provided with comprehensive information about the project’s expectations and risks to make informed decisions about their ability to contribute effectively. They should also be informed about the conditions of their deployment, including the level of healthcare they can expect if they fall ill, the circumstances under which they may be repatriated, available insurance, and whether benefits will be provided to their families in the event of illness or death. Aid workers must receive appropriate training, preparation, and equipment to carry out their missions effectively while minimizing risks. Training should include psychosocial and communication skills, as well as cultural competence to respect and understand local traditions. Organizations have an obligation to provide ongoing support and guidance to their staff during and after their fieldwork. This includes training on managing ethical challenges such as resource allocation, triage, and addressing inequities. A clear chain of authority should be established to provide oversight and guidance. Workers who object to assigned duties should have the opportunity for review and appeal, in accordance with the norms of their organization. Aid workers also have ethical obligations to patients, affected communities, their sponsoring organizations, and themselves. They should participate in all offered training and raise concerns if they feel inadequately prepared. Workers deployed in resource-scarce crisis settings should carefully evaluate their readiness to handle ethical dilemmas that may cause moral or psychological distress. Aid workers must adhere to their assigned roles and responsibilities and should not undertake unauthorized tasks except in extreme circumstances. They should provide timely and accurate information to their sponsoring organizations and local officials. If they exceed their authorized tasks, they may be held accountable under both organizational and local legal standards. Infection control practices must be strictly followed to protect both aid workers and the communities they serve. Workers should adhere to recommended protocols for monitoring symptoms and reporting their health status before, during, and after their service. This includes disclosing any conditions, such as pregnancy, that may affect their ability to perform their duties safely.
